mcqs.question: What is the key difference between cache coherence and memory consistency?
options: They are two names for exactly the same guarantee
Coherence guarantees agreement on the value of a single address across cores; consistency governs what ordering guarantees hold across writes to different addresses
Consistency only applies to single-core systems, while coherence only applies to multicore systems
Coherence is a software-only concern with no hardware involvement
mcqs.explanation: Coherence is per-address agreement; consistency is about cross-address ordering as observed by different cores — a system can be fully coherent yet still allow orderings across different addresses that violate stricter consistency expectations. They aren't the same guarantee, consistency questions specifically arise in multicore systems, and coherence protocols are implemented substantially in hardware.

mcqs.question: Why does most real hardware implement a relaxed consistency model instead of strict sequential consistency?
options: Because sequential consistency is impossible to implement correctly in any hardware
Because enforcing sequential consistency would forbid common performance optimizations like store buffering and reordering independent memory operations, stalling the pipeline
Because relaxed models use less silicon area for the register file
Because sequential consistency only works with single-threaded programs
mcqs.explanation: Relaxed models exist specifically to preserve performance optimizations (store buffers, reordering) that strict SC would forbid, trading some programmer-visible ordering guarantees for hardware speed. SC is implementable (older/simpler machines used it), the trade-off isn't about register-file area, and SC's rules are about ordering across cores, not single-threaded execution.

mcqs.question: In the classic two-writes/two-reads reordering example, why can Core B observe y=1 but still read the old value of x=0?
options: Because x and y are stored on different cache lines, which makes coherence itself fail
Because under a relaxed model, Core A's store buffer can make y=1 visible to other cores before x=1 becomes visible, even though A issued x=1 first in program order
Because Core B's reads are executed by a different core than the one running the writes, which is disallowed
Because sequential consistency is the default on every modern processor
mcqs.explanation: Relaxed models permit a core's writes to become globally visible out of program order via store buffering, which is exactly what produces this seemingly-impossible-but-legal outcome. Coherence per-address still holds (this isn't a coherence failure), cross-core reads/writes are the normal case being analyzed, and most modern processors default to relaxed, not sequential, consistency.

mcqs.question: Why does lock-free code that passes all tests on x86 sometimes fail when deployed on ARM?
options: ARM processors have slower clock speeds that expose timing bugs unrelated to memory ordering

x86's stronger consistency model (TSO) tolerates missing memory fences that a weaker model (ARM's default) does not, so a latent ordering bug was present all along and only manifests once run under a weaker model
ARM processors do not support atomic instructions at all
Lock-free code is fundamentally incompatible with all RISC architectures
mcqs.explanation: The bug is a missing fence that x86's strong TSO model happens to mask; the same code exposes the bug once run on a genuinely weaker model where the reordering it depends against is actually legal and occurs under real contention. It's not about ARM clock speed, ARM does support atomics, and lock-free code isn't inherently incompatible with RISC — it just needs correct fences for the target model.
